lessons.title: Riba, Risk-Sharing and Ethics
lessons.content:
## Finance with a moral framework

**Islamic finance** is finance conducted in line with **Sharia** — Islamic law. It is not merely conventional banking with different labels; it starts from a different set of ethical commitments about what money is for and how risk should be shared.

### The core prohibitions

**Riba — interest.** Charging or paying a guaranteed return on money itself is prohibited. The principle: money should be earned through real trade, assets and effort — not rented out at a fixed rate regardless of outcome.

**Gharar — excessive uncertainty.** Contracts with extreme ambiguity or speculation are prohibited. Terms must be clear, and both sides must understand what they are agreeing to.

**Haram activities.** Funding industries such as alcohol, gambling or weapons is excluded — an ethical screen with some kinship to socially responsible investing in conventional finance.

### The positive principle: risk-sharing

Instead of a lender who profits no matter what, Islamic finance prefers arrangements where **parties share risk and reward** — partners in a venture, buyer and seller of a real asset, insurer and insured pooling risk mutually.

### Why it matters beyond faith

Built on asset-backing and shared risk, the model proved notably resilient in past financial crises, and it attracts interest from people of all backgrounds who want finance tied to real economic activity.

> **One-line summary:** no guaranteed interest, no excessive uncertainty, no harmful industries — and risk shared fairly between the parties.

lessons.title: The Core Contracts
lessons.content:
## How banks profit without charging interest

If interest is off the table, how does Islamic banking work? Through a toolkit of contracts built on trade, partnership and leasing. Three cover most of what you will meet.

### Murabaha — cost-plus sale

The workhorse of Islamic banking. You want to buy a car. The bank **buys the car itself**, then sells it to you at a known markup, paid in instalments. Profit comes from a real sale of a real asset, not from lending money. The price is fixed and transparent from day one.

### Mudaraba — investment partnership

One side provides capital, the other provides expertise and management. Profits are shared at an **agreed ratio**; financial loss falls on the capital provider, while the manager loses their effort. This is the classic structure behind many Islamic investment accounts.

### Musharaka — joint venture

Both sides contribute capital **and** share profits and losses in proportion to ownership. A diminishing version — where one partner gradually buys out the other — is widely used for **home financing** as an alternative to a conventional mortgage.

### The pattern to remember

Every contract ties the bank's return to a **real asset or real venture**. That is the dividing line: profit earned through trade and shared risk, not through renting money.

> Ijara (leasing) and wakala (agency) round out the toolkit — same principle, different shapes.

lessons.title: Sukuk and Takaful
lessons.content:
## The instruments you will actually meet

### Sukuk — the Islamic answer to bonds

A conventional bond pays interest on a loan. A **sukuk** instead gives investors a **share of ownership in a real asset or venture** — a toll road, a building, an aircraft fleet — and pays them a share of the income it generates, such as rent or usage fees.

The difference is structural, not cosmetic: sukuk holders own something tangible, so returns come from an asset's performance. Governments and companies worldwide now issue sukuk to raise money, and the market runs into the hundreds of billions of dollars.

### Takaful — insurance as mutual protection

Conventional insurance sells risk transfer to a company for a premium. **Takaful** works as a **mutual pool**: participants contribute to a common fund that pays members' claims, managed on their behalf. Surpluses can be returned to participants, and the fund invests only in Sharia-compliant assets.

### Why these two matter

Sukuk and takaful show the principles from module one operating at full scale: asset-backing, risk-sharing and ethical screening — packaged as instruments familiar enough for global markets to trade.

> **Spot the pattern again:** sukuk = own the asset, share its income. Takaful = pool the risk, share the outcome.

lessons.title: Islamic Finance in the World Today
lessons.content:
## A global industry, still growing

Islamic finance is a **multi-trillion-dollar global industry**. Its heartlands are the Gulf states and Malaysia, but Islamic banks, sukuk listings and Sharia-compliant funds operate in financial centres from London to Singapore — and several conventional banks run Islamic windows alongside their regular business.

### Who keeps it honest?

Each institution has a **Sharia board** — scholars who review products and certify compliance. Bodies such as **AAOIFI** and the **IFSB** publish standards that harmonise practice across countries, though interpretations still differ between markets. When you evaluate an Islamic financial product, the Sharia board's certification is the first thing to look for.

### Where it meets what you already know

- **Ethical screening** overlaps with SRI and ESG — several Islamic indices sit comfortably beside sustainability indices.
- **Asset-backing** echoes the green bond idea: money tied to something real and traceable.
- **Risk-sharing** resembles the partnership logic of impact investing.

### The challenges, honestly

Standardisation across countries is incomplete, some products are criticised for imitating conventional interest too closely in practice, and awareness outside Muslim-majority markets remains low. All three are active areas of reform.

> Whatever your background, Islamic finance is worth understanding: it is one of the clearest working examples of finance redesigned around an explicit ethical framework.

choices: Interest — a guaranteed return on money itself, which is prohibited
questions.explain: Riba is interest. Islamic finance earns profit through real trade, assets and shared risk instead.

questions.q: In a murabaha arrangement, the bank…
choices: Buys the asset itself and sells it to you at a known markup in instalments
questions.explain: Murabaha is a cost-plus sale: profit comes from selling a real asset at a transparent markup, not from lending money.

questions.q: Mudaraba and musharaka are both built on…
questions.explain: Both are partnership structures. Mudaraba pairs capital with expertise; musharaka has both sides contribute capital and share outcomes.

questions.q: How does a sukuk differ from a conventional bond?
choices: Holders own a share of a real asset and earn its income, rather than interest on a loan
It can only be bought by governments
questions.explain: Sukuk = ownership in an asset with income from its performance. Bonds = a loan paying interest. The structure, not just the label, differs.

choices: Selling risk to a company for profit
Participants pooling contributions in a mutual fund that pays members' claims
questions.explain: Takaful is mutual: members contribute to a common pool, surpluses can be returned, and the fund invests only in Sharia-compliant assets.

questions.q: Who certifies that a financial product is Sharia-compliant?
choices: A Sharia board of scholars, guided by standards bodies like AAOIFI
questions.explain: Each institution has a Sharia board; bodies like AAOIFI and IFSB harmonise standards across markets.
